experiment.intervention: Only native output format: FORMAT JSONEachRow vs FORMAT Null, same PromQL SQL up to FORMAT, stock RAW UUID v11
experiment.evaluation: 3 daily timestamps, 3-48 points across each query case
experiment.phases: For each case JSON/Null/Null/JSON, 2 warmups +24 measured per phase, 416 total including warmups, single request at a time
experiment.correctness: All JSON phases compared complete nonempty PromQL labels/time/float values against initial JSON oracle; Null phases asserted zero HTTP bytes and unchanged QueryFinish read_rows and SelectedMarks. Same physical TAGS/TimeRanges/SAMPLES one-part rows, marks and bytes before/after.
experiment.controls: All JSON/JSON p50 and CPU drift <=25%; use observed drift to avoid claiming 0-2ms effects are robust
experiment.query_logging: QueryFinish CPU OSCPUVirtualTimeMicroseconds and memory; 4Hz RSS not used; process RSS before/after outside timed phases
experiment.profiler: One measured CPU trace, hot leaves, folded stacks and processors_profile_log per format per case. All trace categories populated, but one representative query is not the median and operator-work sums overlap across threads.

findings: On selective namespace, suppressing 191 HTTP output bytes reduced median CPU only 1.077ms out of 94.337ms (~1.14%); 1.079ms p50 wall reduction is close to 0.84% JSON/JSON wall drift and not a universal speedup.
On burst15, suppressing 767 bytes left median CPU unchanged (67.899 vs68.010ms), while both formats read 66,016 rows and 87 selected marks.

On broad nodes, FORMAT Null was slower by 28.775ms CPU and 21.0ms wall despite equal selected rows/marks and physical parts. This is an execution/pipeline effect or measurement characteristic, not negative serializer cost; format change is not a pure serialization microbenchmark.
On all pods, median CPU differs by only 2.116ms in the direction opposite expected JSON overhead, with exactly equal query read rows/marks.

CPU trace shows selective namespace 45/90 CPU samples from read/decode and representative MergeTreeSelect(ReadPool) work 40.874ms; broad-node 128/413 samples grid aggregation, 121 expression, 54 read, 42 tag registration; broad-pod 131/408 grid and 107 tag registration. These are representative single-query statistical samples, not end-to-end wall shares.

Inspect source: NullOutputFormat::consume(Chunk) is empty but source documentation says query is still processed; output bytes ==0. JSONEachRow format converts column fields. Same read_rows/selected_marks in R17 confirms stable physical read path but not exactly identical operator execution.

R03 optimized VM1.134 is 3-41x faster than stock O1 CH on matched 3d fixture. R17 only rules out JSON output as a dominant plausible cause for the two narrow selectors. It does not explain cross-engine fixed overhead or prove compiler-normalized gap.
limitations: No production-normalized VM comparison in this run; previous R03 compares stock O1/glibc to optimized VM release.
Changing FORMAT can change output-pipeline scheduling; `cpu(json) - cpu(null)` is a diagnostic format-dependent delta, not a pure JSON function cost.
Trace sampler counts for one query per arm are statistical, while median QueryFinish CPU and wall are repeated trial metrics.
Data has aligned node starts; no staleness/late-writes; query response output 3-48 samples; results do not apply to large PromQL result payloads.
R05 owns ID mark selection, R07 owns day-cover metadata sidecar, R03 owns VM comparison, R14 owns grid rollup, R15 owns calendar partitions; R17 did not modify or duplicate those.
next_action: Use R17 representative trace to target read/decode and grid/tag registration CPU, but do not repeat existing R05/R07/R14 tests. Investigate source-exact SAMPLES column codec efficiency or operator buffer materialization (e.g. ALP and memset) as independent bounded R18 question before new C++ build.
